title: OF TREATIES OF COMMERCE.
paragraphs: Treaties of Commerce

Sometimes a nation signs a treaty agreeing to admit certain goods from one foreign country while barring those same goods from everyone else, or agreeing to exempt one country's goods from duties that it still charges on everyone else's. When that happens, the favoured country, or at least its merchants and manufacturers, is bound to gain a great deal from the deal. Those merchants and manufacturers effectively enjoy a kind of monopoly in the country that treats them so generously. That country becomes a market for their goods that is both larger and more profitable. It is larger because, with rival nations' goods either shut out or taxed more heavily, it absorbs a greater quantity of theirs. It is more profitable because the favoured country's merchants, holding their near-monopoly, can often sell at a higher price than they could if they had to face open competition from every other nation.

Yet however much such treaties benefit the merchants and manufacturers of the favoured country, they necessarily hurt those of the country granting the favour. That country has handed a foreign nation a monopoly against itself, so its own people must frequently pay more for the foreign goods they need than they would if competition were open to all. And since the home country uses part of its own output to buy those foreign goods, that part of its output must be sold more cheaply. When two things are traded for each other, one being cheaper is just the flip side of the other being dearer; they are really the same fact stated twice. So the exchangeable value of the favouring country's annual output is likely to shrink with every treaty of this sort. Even so, this shrinkage hardly amounts to an outright loss; it is only a reduction in the gain the country might otherwise have made. Although it sells its goods more cheaply than it might, it probably still does not sell them below cost, nor, as happens with bounties, at a price that fails to repay the capital used to bring them to market along with the ordinary profit on that capital. The trade could not last long if it did. So even the favouring country may still come out ahead from the trade, just less than it would under free competition.

Some commercial treaties, however, have been thought beneficial on grounds quite different from these. A trading country has sometimes granted a foreign nation this kind of monopoly against its own interest because it expected that, over the whole of their trade, it would sell more each year than it bought, with the difference flowing back to it in gold and silver. It is on this reasoning that the commerce treaty between England and Portugal, concluded in 1703 by Mr Methuen, has been so highly praised. What follows is a word-for-word translation of that treaty, which has only three articles.

ARTICLE I. His sacred royal majesty of Portugal promises, in his own name and that of his successors, to admit into Portugal forever after the woollen cloths and other woollen manufactures of the British, just as he did before the law banned them, on one condition:

ARTICLE II. Namely, that her sacred royal majesty of Great Britain shall be obliged, in her own name and that of her successors, to admit into Britain forever after the wines grown in Portugal. At no time, whether Britain and France are at peace or at war, shall anything more be charged on these wines, under the name of customs or duty or under any other heading, directly or indirectly, whether they enter Great Britain in pipes, hogsheads, or other casks, than is charged on the same quantity or measure of French wine, less one-third of that customs or duty. But if at any point this one-third reduction is in any way withheld or undermined, the sacred royal majesty of Portugal shall be fully entitled to ban the woollen cloths and other British woollen manufactures once again.

ARTICLE III. The most excellent lord plenipotentiaries promise, and pledge themselves, that the masters named above will ratify this treaty, and that the ratifications will be exchanged within two months.

By this treaty the crown of Portugal commits to admitting English woollens on the same terms as before the ban, that is, not to raise the duties paid up to that point. But it does not commit to admitting them on any better terms than it gives any other nation, France or Holland, for instance. The crown of Great Britain, by contrast, commits to admitting Portuguese wines while charging only two-thirds of the duty levied on French wines, the wines most likely to compete with them. To that extent, then, the treaty plainly favours Portugal and works against Great Britain.

Yet it has been hailed as a masterpiece of English commercial policy. Each year Portugal receives from Brazil more gold than its domestic economy can absorb, whether as coin or as plate. The surplus is too valuable to sit idle and locked away in vaults, and since it can find no profitable use at home, it has to be sent abroad, despite any ban, and exchanged for something more useful at home. A large share of it comes to England every year, paid either for English goods or for the goods of other European nations that take their returns through England. Mr Barretti was told that the weekly packet-boat from Lisbon carries, on average, more than £50,000 in gold to England each week. That figure was probably inflated. It would come to more than £2,600,000 a year, which is more than Brazil is thought to supply.

A few years ago our merchants were annoyed with the Portuguese crown. Certain privileges that crown had granted them, not by treaty but as a free favour, probably at their request and in return for much greater favours, namely defence and protection from the British crown, had been either broken or withdrawn. So the very people usually keenest to celebrate the Portugal trade were then inclined to paint it as less advantageous than it had generally been assumed to be. They claimed that by far the greater part, nearly all, of this yearly gold inflow was not really on Britain's account but on that of other European nations, since the fruits and wines Portugal sent to Britain each year roughly matched the value of the British goods shipped there.

But suppose the whole inflow really were on Britain's account, and that it came to an even larger sum than Mr Barretti imagines. Even so, this trade would be no more advantageous than any other in which, for the same value sent out, we received an equal value of consumable goods in return.

Only a very small part of this inflow, surely, is used to add each year to the kingdom's stock of plate or coin. All the rest has to be sent abroad and exchanged for consumable goods of one kind or another. But if those consumable goods were bought directly with the products of English industry, England would gain more than by first using that output to buy Portuguese gold and then using that gold to buy the consumable goods. A direct foreign trade in consumer goods is always better than a roundabout one, and bringing the same value of foreign goods to the home market takes far less capital the direct way than the indirect way. So if England had put a smaller share of its industry into making goods for the Portuguese market and a larger share into making goods for the markets where the consumables Britain wants can actually be had, it would have been better off. Obtaining both the gold it needs for its own use and the consumer goods would, this way, tie up far less capital than at present. There would then be spare capital free for other purposes, to set additional industry in motion and produce a greater output each year.

Even if Britain were shut out of the Portugal trade entirely, it would have little trouble obtaining all the gold it needs each year, whether for plate, for coin, or for foreign trade. Gold, like every other commodity, can always be got somewhere or other for its price by anyone with that price to pay. Besides, Portugal's annual gold surplus would still be sent abroad, and if Britain did not carry it off, some other nation would, glad to resell it at its price just as Britain does now. True, buying gold from Portugal means buying it at first hand, whereas buying it from any nation but Spain would mean buying it at second hand and perhaps paying a little more. But that difference is surely too trivial to merit public concern.

Almost all our gold, it is said, comes from Portugal, while with other nations the balance of trade is either against us or only slightly in our favour. But we should bear in mind that the more gold we import from one country, the less we must import from all the rest. The effective demand for gold, like that for every other commodity, is limited in each country to a certain amount. If nine-tenths of that amount comes from one country, only a tenth is left to come from everyone else. What is more, the more gold imported each year from particular countries beyond what is needed for plate and coin, the more must be re-exported to others. And the more that most trifling object of modern policy, the balance of trade, seems to favour us with certain countries, the more it must necessarily run against us with many others.

It was on this foolish idea, though, that England could not survive without the Portugal trade, that near the end of the recent war France and Spain, claiming no offence or provocation, demanded that the king of Portugal close all his ports to British ships and, to enforce the closure, admit French or Spanish garrisons into them. Had the king of Portugal accepted the humiliating terms his brother-in-law the king of Spain offered, Britain would have been relieved of something far worse than the loss of the Portugal trade: the burden of propping up a very weak ally, so unequipped for his own defence that the whole power of England, even if aimed at that single task, could scarcely have protected him for one more campaign. Losing the Portugal trade would no doubt have badly inconvenienced the merchants then engaged in it, who might have needed a year or two to find another equally profitable use for their capital, and in that, probably, would have consisted the whole of the harm England could have suffered from this celebrated stroke of commercial policy.

The large annual import of gold and silver is meant neither for plate nor for coin but for foreign trade. A roundabout foreign trade in consumer goods can be carried on more profitably with these metals than with almost any other goods. Because they are the universal instruments of commerce, they are taken in exchange for all commodities more readily than any other goods. And because they pack great value into small bulk, they cost less to ship back and forth than almost any other merchandise, and lose less of their value in transit. So of all the commodities bought in one foreign country purely to be sold or swapped again for other goods in another, none are as convenient as gold and silver. The main advantage of the Portugal trade lies in how it eases all the various roundabout foreign trades in consumer goods carried on in Great Britain, and though this is not a decisive advantage, it is certainly a considerable one.

It seems clear enough that whatever annual addition can reasonably be supposed to be made to the kingdom's plate or coin would call for only a very small yearly import of gold and silver. And even without any direct trade with Portugal, that small quantity could always be obtained easily enough somewhere or other.

Although the goldsmiths' trade in Great Britain is quite large, by far the greater part of the new plate they sell each year is made from old plate melted down. So the net yearly addition to the kingdom's total stock of plate cannot be great, and would require only a very small annual import.

It is the same with coin. Nobody, I think, imagines that even the greater part of the annual coinage, which for ten years running before the recent reform of the gold coin came to over £800,000 a year in gold, was a net yearly addition to the money already in circulation in the kingdom. In a country where the government pays the cost of coining, the value of the coin, even when it holds its full standard weight of gold and silver, can never be much above that of the same quantity of those metals uncoined, since it takes only the trouble of going to the mint, and perhaps a delay of a few weeks, to turn any amount of uncoined gold and silver into an equal amount of coined metal. But in every country most of the coin in circulation is almost always worn down, or otherwise fallen below its standard. In Great Britain, before the recent reform, this was very much the case: the gold was more than two per cent, and the silver more than eight per cent, below standard weight. Now, if forty-four and a half guineas at full standard weight, holding a pound weight of gold, could buy very little more than a pound weight of uncoined gold, then forty-four and a half guineas short of part of their weight could not buy a pound weight, and something had to be added to make up the shortfall. So the market price of gold bullion, instead of matching the mint price of £46:14:6, stood at about £47:14s, and sometimes around £48. Yet when most of the coin was in this degraded state, forty-four and a half guineas fresh from the mint would buy no more goods in the market than any other ordinary guineas, because once they reached a merchant's till and mingled with other money, they could not be told apart again without more trouble than the difference was worth. Like other guineas, they were worth no more than £46:14:6. Thrown into the melting pot, however, they yielded, with no noticeable loss, a pound weight of standard gold, which could be sold at any time for between £47:14s and £48, in gold or silver, as fit for all the purposes of coin as the metal that had been melted down. There was thus an obvious profit in melting down freshly coined money, and it was done so quickly that no government precaution could stop it. The mint's work, on this account, was rather like Penelope's web: what was done by day was undone by night. The mint was employed not so much in adding to the coin each day as in replacing the very best of it, which was melted down each day.

If the private people who carry their gold and silver to the mint had to pay for the coining themselves, it would raise the value of those metals, just as workmanship raises the value of plate. Coined gold and silver would then be worth more than uncoined. A seignorage, provided it was not excessive, would add its full value to the bullion, because, since the government everywhere holds the sole right to coin, no coin can reach the market more cheaply than the government chooses to allow. If the duty were excessive, though, that is, far above the real cost of the labour and expense of coining, then the wide gap between the value of bullion and that of coin might tempt counterfeiters at home and abroad to flood the market with so much false money that the value of the government's money would fall. In France, however, even though the seignorage is eight per cent, no real trouble of this sort arises from it. The dangers a counterfeiter faces everywhere, if he lives in the country whose coin he forges, and that his agents or correspondents face, if he lives abroad, are far too great to be run for the sake of a profit of six or seven per cent.

In France the seignorage raises the value of the coin by more than the proportion of pure gold it contains. Thus, by the edict of January 1726, the mint price of fine gold of twenty-four carats was fixed at seven hundred and forty livres, nine sous, and one and one-eleventh denier per mark of eight Paris ounces. {See Dictionnaire des Monnoies, vol. ii, article Seigneurage, p. 439, par 81. Abbot de Bazinghen, Conseiller-Commissaire en la Cour des Monnoies à Paris.} French gold coin, allowing for the mint's tolerance, contains twenty-one and three-quarter carats of fine gold and two and one-quarter carats of alloy. So the mark of standard gold is worth only about six hundred and seventy-one livres ten deniers. But in France this mark of standard gold is coined into thirty louis d'ors of twenty-four livres each, or seven hundred and twenty livres. The coining therefore raises the value of a mark of standard gold bullion by the difference between six hundred and seventy-one livres ten deniers and seven hundred and twenty livres, that is, by forty-eight livres, nineteen sous, and two deniers.

A seignorage will in many cases wipe out entirely, and in all cases reduce, the profit of melting down new coin. That profit always comes from the gap between the amount of bullion the common currency ought to contain and the amount it actually does contain. If this gap is smaller than the seignorage, there will be a loss instead of a profit. If it equals the seignorage, there will be neither profit nor loss. If it is larger than the seignorage, there will be some profit, but less than if there were no seignorage. Suppose, for instance, that before the recent reform of the gold coin there had been a seignorage of five per cent on the coinage: melting down the gold coin would then have brought a loss of three per cent. With a seignorage of two per cent, there would have been neither profit nor loss. With one per cent, there would have been a profit of only one per cent rather than two. So wherever money is taken by count and not by weight, a seignorage is the most effective deterrent against melting the coin down, and, for the same reason, against exporting it. It is the best and heaviest pieces that are usually melted or exported, because those yield the largest profits.

The law encouraging coinage by making it duty-free was first passed in the reign of Charles II for a limited time, then renewed by various extensions until 1769, when it was made permanent. To refill their vaults with money, the Bank of England often has to carry bullion to the mint, and the directors probably reasoned that it suited their interest better for the government to bear the cost of coining than to bear it themselves. It was probably to oblige this great company that the government agreed to make the law permanent. But should the practice of weighing gold ever fall out of use, as it is very likely to, given how inconvenient it is, and should English gold coin come to be taken by count, as it was before the recent recoinage, this great company may find that here, as on some other occasions, it has rather badly misjudged its own interest.

Before the recent recoinage, when England's gold currency was two per cent below its standard weight and there was no seignorage, the coin was two per cent below the value of the standard gold bullion it ought to have contained. So when this great company bought gold bullion to have it coined, it had to pay two per cent more for the bullion than the coin was worth once minted. But had there been a seignorage of two per cent on the coining, the common gold currency, though two per cent short of its standard weight, would still have equalled in value the standard gold it ought to have contained, the value of the workmanship making up for the loss of weight. The company would, of course, have had the seignorage to pay; at two per cent, its loss on the whole transaction would have been two per cent, exactly the same as it actually was, and no greater.

Had the seignorage been five per cent and the gold currency only two per cent below its standard weight, the bank would in that case have gained three per cent on the price of the bullion. But since it would have had a five per cent seignorage to pay on the coining, its loss on the whole transaction would again have come to exactly two per cent.

Had the seignorage been only one per cent and the gold currency two per cent below standard weight, the bank would in that case have lost only one per cent on the price of the bullion. But since it would also have had a one per cent seignorage to pay, its loss on the whole transaction would have been exactly two per cent, just as in every other case.

If there were a reasonable seignorage while at the same time the coin held its full standard weight, as it has done very nearly since the recent recoinage, then whatever the bank lost on the seignorage it would gain on the price of the bullion, and whatever it gained on the price of the bullion it would lose on the seignorage. It would therefore neither lose nor gain on the whole transaction, and would be, here as in all the earlier cases, in exactly the same position as if there were no seignorage at all.

When a tax on a commodity is moderate enough not to encourage smuggling, the merchant who deals in that commodity advances the tax but does not really pay it, since he recovers it in the price. The tax falls in the end on the last buyer, the consumer. But money is a commodity in which every person is a merchant. Nobody buys it except to sell it again, and with money there is, in the ordinary way, no last buyer or consumer. So when the tax on coinage is moderate enough not to encourage counterfeiting, everyone advances the tax but nobody finally pays it, because everyone recovers it in the raised value of the coin.

A moderate seignorage, then, would never add to the expense of the bank, or of any other private people who carry their bullion to the mint to be coined, and the lack of a moderate seignorage never reduces that expense. Whether there is a seignorage or not, if the currency holds its full standard weight, the coining costs nobody anything. And if the currency is below that weight, the coining must always cost the difference between the bullion that ought to be in it and the bullion that actually is.

So when the government pays the cost of coinage, it not only incurs some small expense but also forgoes some small revenue it could collect through a proper duty, while neither the bank nor any other private people gain in the slightest from this useless act of public generosity.

Still, the bank's directors would probably be reluctant to accept a seignorage on the strength of a line of reasoning that promises them no gain and only claims to protect them from loss. In the present state of the gold coin, and as long as it is taken by weight, they would certainly gain nothing from such a change. But if the practice of weighing the gold coin should ever fall out of use, as it very likely will, and if the gold coin should ever sink into the same degraded state it was in before the recent recoinage, the gain, or rather the savings, the bank would make from a seignorage would probably be very large. The Bank of England is the only company that sends any considerable quantity of bullion to the mint, and the burden of the annual coinage falls entirely, or almost entirely, on it. If this annual coinage had only to repair the unavoidable losses and ordinary wear and tear of the coin, it could rarely exceed fifty thousand, or at most a hundred thousand pounds. But when the coin is worn below its standard weight, the annual coinage must on top of this fill up the great gaps that exportation and the melting pot keep making in the circulating coin. It was for this reason that, during the ten or twelve years just before the recent reform of the gold coin, the annual coinage averaged more than £850,000. Yet had there been a seignorage of four or five per cent on the gold coin, it would probably, even in the state things were then in, have put an effective stop to both exportation and the melting pot. Instead of losing about two and a half per cent each year on the bullion coined into more than eight hundred and fifty thousand pounds, that is, an annual loss of more than £21,250, the bank would probably not have lost a tenth of that.

The revenue parliament sets aside to cover the cost of coinage is only fourteen thousand pounds a year, and the real cost to the government, the fees of the mint officers, does not usually, I am assured, exceed half that sum. Saving so very small a sum, or even gaining another that could not be much larger, may seem too trifling to deserve the serious attention of government. But saving eighteen or twenty thousand pounds a year, should an event occur that is not unlikely, that has happened often before, and that is very likely to happen again, is surely well worth the serious attention even of so great a company as the Bank of England.

Some of the foregoing arguments and observations might perhaps have fitted better in those chapters of the first book that deal with the origin and use of money and with the difference between the real and the nominal price of commodities. But since the law encouraging coinage springs from those common prejudices introduced by the mercantile system, I judged it more fitting to keep them for this chapter. Nothing could suit the spirit of that system better than a kind of bounty on the production of money, the very thing it supposes to constitute the wealth of every nation. It is one of its many admirable contrivances for enriching the country.
